dispositions.sentence: Second-century rival the proto-orthodox defined themselves against
dispositions.reason: Carried by three new argued-against links: tertullian-s-voice (Against Marcion, anf03 22569-22610), greek-apologists-second-century (Justin, 1 Apol. 26, anf01 14943-14945) and post-apostolic-house-church (expulsion and Polycarp, anf03 29239-29241, anf01 39871-39884).

dispositions.sentence: In 144 the Roman church expelled him and returned his money.
dispositions.reason: The Roman church before 200 belongs to post-apostolic-house-church (region includes Rome; it 'continued as' roman-church-third-century). Expulsion and returned money: Tertullian, Adv. Marc. IV.4 (anf03 29239-29241) and De praescr. 30 (21338-21340). The year 144 is not in any vendored text and is disputed (Moll 2010, cited in Build/worlds/pahc/CiC_W1_Doc01_World_Identification_FINAL.md line 128), so the date is qualified.

dispositions.sentence: Everything we have comes through the men who wrote to refute him, above all Tertullian, whose Against Marcion runs to five books.
dispositions.reason: Against Marcion, five books, vendored in anf03_tertullian.xml from line 22297; quotes at 22569-22570 and 22609-22610.

dispositions.sentence: After the Roman church expelled him in 144 and returned his money, he built a rival network of congregations with its own edited Scripture - a version of Luke and ten letters of Paul, stripped of what he judged to be Jewish corruption.
dispositions.reason: Same link and evidence as the longDescription sentence; the year is qualified the same way. Splitting the sentence also raises its reading ease.

dispositions.sentence: Congregations that had never needed to specify which books counted as Scripture discovered that they now had to, and the confession of one God, maker of heaven and earth, whose Son truly took flesh, was hammered into its sharpest early form in argument against him.
dispositions.reason: The opponents here are the movements already linked (Tertullian, Justin, the Roman house churches); this sentence echoes those links. The argument itself is in Adv. Marc. I.2 (two Gods, anf03 22609) and 1 Apol. 26 (God as maker, anf01 14945). 'Sharpest early form' is a judgment, not a relationship claim.

dispositions.sentence: How far he actually caused the New Testament canon rather than accelerated a process already under way is still debated by historians.
dispositions.reason: Canon formation is a process, not a movement. The sentence already states the debate plainly; the pahc Doc_01 (line 128) cites Lieu (2015) on Marcion's role.

dispositions.sentence: Justin Martyr — wrote against him within Marcion's own lifetime, in a work now lost
dispositions.reason: Added (not in the inventory). Justin's First Apology 26 (anf01 14943-14945) and Dialogue 35 (19254-19255) survive and name Marcion and the 'Marcians'. The voices line is not wrong (the Syntagma is lost) but undersells what survives; flagged on the link, not changed.

dispositions.sentence: Irenaeus of Lyons — one of the earliest to answer him, and the source for the story that Polycarp, meeting Marcion in the street, called him 'the firstborn of Satan'
dispositions.reason: Added. Irenaeus has no entry (Lyons is in no census movement), but Polycarp of Smyrna belongs to post-apostolic-house-church; Adv. haer. III.3.4 (anf01 39882-39884) carries the 'first-born of Satan' exchange. Irenaeus does not say it happened in the street.

dispositions.sentence: Rivals the early traditions anathematized and were shaped by
dispositions.reason: The early churches are post-apostolic-house-church, greek-apologists-second-century and tertullian-s-voice, each now linked. No vendored text records a formal anathema in the period; what they show is expulsion (De praescr. 30, anf03 21338-21339) and written refutation, so 'anathematized' becomes 'cast out and wrote against'.

dispositions.sentence: Valentinus was an Alexandrian teacher who came to Rome around 136 and, according to Tertullian, was nearly elected bishop there.
dispositions.reason: Adv. Val. 4 (anf03 43109-43114): Valentinus 'had expected to become a bishop' and broke with the church when another won it on a confessor's claim. 'Nearly elected' and 'there' go beyond the passage. Arrival under Hyginus: Adv. haer. III.4.3 (anf01 39969).

dispositions.sentence: Along with related currents around teachers like Basilides, they mostly did not build rival churches: they sat in ordinary congregations and offered their teaching as the deeper meaning available to those ready for it, which is precisely what alarmed bishops like Irenaeus, whose five-volume Against Heresies of about 180 was written to drag the system into the open and refute it.
dispositions.reason: Basilides has no entry. Supported: Justin, Dial. 35 names 'Basilidians' beside the Valentinians (anf01 19254-19255).

dispositions.sentence: Along with related currents around teachers like Basilides, they mostly did not build rival churches: they sat in ordinary congregations and offered their teaching as the deeper meaning available to those ready for it, which is precisely what alarmed bishops like Irenaeus, whose five-volume Against Heresies of about 180 was written to drag the system into the open and refute it.
dispositions.reason: Irenaeus of Lyons has no entry. Supported: Against Heresies in five books is vendored in anf01 (Book I preface from line 29785, which says he writes to expose their teaching); Adv. haer. III.3.3 names Eleutherius as the present bishop of Rome (line 39849), which fits c. 180.

dispositions.sentence: Valentinus was an Alexandrian teacher who came to Rome around 136 ... they sat in ordinary congregations
dispositions.reason: Added. The Roman congregations of 136-160 are post-apostolic-house-church. Irenaeus: Valentinus in Rome from Hyginus to Anicetus (anf01 39969); Polycarp turned many from Valentinus and Marcion at Rome (39871-39873). Tertullian: expelled more than once (anf03 21338-21339).

dispositions.sentence: First, the shape of what became orthodox Christianity was set partly by the labor of answering them.
dispositions.reason: Echoes the three new argued-against links (post-apostolic-house-church, greek-apologists-second-century, tertullian-s-voice); the 'partly' keeps it a judgment, not a stated relationship.

dispositions.sentence: The ground third-century Antioch stands on, eighty years before it starts, and the seedbed of the controversy the Homoian and Anomoean disputes later assess.
dispositions.reason: Existing Documented link (Theodoret HE I.5; Philostorgius II.14). The sentence itself was garbled and used internal language ('assess'); rewritten.

dispositions.sentence: The ground third-century Antioch stands on, eighty years before it starts, and the seedbed of the controversy the Homoian and Anomoean disputes later assess.

dispositions.sentence: Its relation to modalist-monarchianism is symmetry rather than descent: Paul's adoptionism and Sabellius' modalism are the two opposite ways of declining the account of the Son that the century was working out.
dispositions.reason: A comparison that expressly denies a relationship, so no link. The 2026-11-06 pass found no vendored text setting Paul and the modalists in contact (README, wanted texts). Only the raw id is changed.

dispositions.sentence: The teaching at issue was that Christ was a man in whom the Word had come to dwell rather than the Word made flesh - the reading later called adoptionist.
dispositions.reason: A teaching, not a movement. The charges are in the synodal letter, HE VII.30 (npnf201 from line 41993).

dispositions.sentence: Paul of Samosata was bishop of the greatest city in the Roman East and, on the account of the council that removed him, a salaried official of the Palmyrene administration that then governed it.
dispositions.reason: Not a movement relationship, but the attribution overstates. The synodal letter says only that Paul preferred the title ducenarius (HE VII.30.8, npnf201 42104-42105). The Palmyrene post is the editor's inference (note at 42105), consistent with Athanasius's report that Zenobia supported Paul.

dispositions.sentence: The council could not make the deposition stick, because the civil power was Palmyrene and Paul had its favor; he went only when Aurelian retook the city in 272 and settled the question of who owned the church building by asking which claimant was in communion with the bishops of Italy and Rome, which is the first time a Roman emperor adjudicated a Christian dispute.
dispositions.reason: Aurelian was a pagan emperor in 272; imperial-juridical-christianity begins in 312 with the Christian empire, so no link. The ruling is in HE VII.30.19 (npnf201 42326-42328). 'The first time' is an inference from silence, left as is.

dispositions.sentence: he went only when Aurelian retook the city in 272 and settled the question of who owned the church building by asking which claimant was in communion with the bishops of Italy and Rome
dispositions.reason: Added. New in-contact link: the synod's letter is addressed to Dionysius, bishop of Rome (HE VII.30.2, npnf201 42003-42006), and Aurelian deferred to the bishops of Italy and Rome (42326-42328).

dispositions.sentence: In 268 or thereabouts the bishops of Syria and Asia Minor met at Antioch for the third time in a few years to deal with their own metropolitan.
dispositions.reason: Added. New in-contact link: Eusebius names Gregory and Athenodorus of Pontus among the bishops who gathered at Antioch (HE VII.27.2-28.1, npnf201 41859-41874). Palestinian bishops also signed (Hymenaeus, Theotecnus, line 42014), but the text says 'Syria and Asia Minor', so no Palestine link is drafted.

dispositions.sentence: A generation later, in the same city, a presbyter named Lucian worked over the text of the Greek Bible and taught a circle of students - Arius among them - who afterwards used his name as a badge.
dispositions.reason: Existing Documented link.

dispositions.sentence: The council's rejection of the word 'homoousios' as something Paul had misused is a large part of why that same word was still suspect at Nicaea, sixty years later.
dispositions.reason: Nicaea is a council, not a movement. The only vendored witness is Athanasius, On the Councils 43-45 (npnf204 58972-59060), written c. 359, reporting what bishops wary of the word said; he had not seen the letter himself. Nothing vendored shows the point raised at Nicaea in 325.

dispositions.sentence: The word homoousios - one substance - seems to have been rejected here as something Paul had misused, which is a large part of why its adoption at Nicaea in 325 was so contentious, and why Eastern bishops who were not Arians could still be uneasy about it.
dispositions.reason: Same evidence as the why-field sentence. The second half (later unease) is supported by On the Councils 43; the first (contention at Nicaea) is not, so it goes.

dispositions.sentence: And Lucian's school gave the Arian party its leadership and its self-description: Arius wrote to Eusebius of Nicomedia as one Lucianist to another.
dispositions.reason: Existing Documented link; its quotes match the sentence.

dispositions.sentence: Within fifty years the same provinces were the base of the bishops who ran the Homoian church of the West: Valens of Mursa and Ursacius of Singidunum, the Sirmium creeds of the 350s, and finally Palladius of Ratiaria, deposed at Aquileia in 381 by a council that came up from Italy to do it.
dispositions.reason: Existing Widely Accepted link (Athanasius, Apol. c. Ar. 48; Hanson 1988).

dispositions.sentence: Victorinus' recapitulation reading of the Apocalypse - that the seals, trumpets and bowls narrate the same events over again rather than a sequence of them - passed through Jerome's revision into Tyconius and Augustine and became the standard Western reading of the book.
dispositions.reason: The reading did survive Jerome's revision: the received text says what recurs in the bowls 'is not said as if it occurred twice' (anf07, Victorinus on Apoc. 8). But it cannot have reached Tyconius through that revision: Tyconius wrote c. 380 (Burkitt edition header), before it.

dispositions.reason: Tyconius has no entry. His rule of recapitulation is vendored (tyconius_liber-regularum_burkitt1894.txt) but does not name Victorinus; treated as qualify in the same prose change.

prose_changes.new: Valentinus was an Alexandrian teacher who came to Rome around 136. Tertullian says he hoped to become a bishop, and broke with the church when a confessor was chosen instead.
prose_changes.reason: Tertullian, Against the Valentinians 4 (anf03_tertullian.xml 43109-43114) says Valentinus 'had expected to become a bishop' and broke with the church when another won it on a confessor's claim. Nothing there says he was nearly elected, and the passage does not name the see.

prose_changes.old: The ground third-century Antioch stands on, eighty years before it starts, and the seedbed of the controversy the Homoian and Anomoean disputes later assess. Its relation to modalist-monarchianism is symmetry rather than descent: Paul's adoptionism and Sabellius' modalism are the two opposite ways of declining the account of the Son that the century was working out.
prose_changes.new: Third-century Antioch was the seedbed of the fourth-century quarrel over the Son. Lucian's pupils led the Arian party, and three of them later taught Aetius, the first Anomoean teacher. Its tie to modalist monarchianism is a mirror, not a line of descent. Paul's adoptionism and Sabellius' modalism were opposite ways of refusing the account of the Son that the century was working out.
prose_changes.reason: The first sentence was garbled ('stands on, eighty years before it starts') and used internal language ('assess', a raw movement id). The rewrite states what the sources show: Lucian's pupils among the Arian leaders (Theodoret HE I.5; Philostorgius II.14) and as Aetius's teachers (Philostorgius III.15). The modalist sentence keeps its meaning with the raw id replaced by a name.

prose_changes.old: Paul of Samosata was bishop of the greatest city in the Roman East and, on the account of the council that removed him, a salaried official of the Palmyrene administration that then governed it.
prose_changes.new: Paul of Samosata was bishop of the greatest city in the Roman East. The council that removed him says he liked to be called ducenarius, a salaried official's title, probably held under the Palmyrene rulers of the city.
prose_changes.reason: The synodal letter (Eusebius HE VII.30.8, npnf201 42104-42105) says only that Paul preferred to be called ducenarius; the tie to the Palmyrene administration is the editor's inference (note at 42105), backed by Athanasius's report that Zenobia supported Paul.

prose_changes.old: The council's rejection of the word 'homoousios' as something Paul had misused is a large part of why that same word was still suspect at Nicaea, sixty years later.
prose_changes.new: In the 350s, bishops wary of Nicaea's word 'homoousios' pointed back to this council. They said it had turned the word down, and Athanasius had to explain why.
prose_changes.reason: The only vendored witness is Athanasius, On the Councils 43-45 (npnf204 58972-59060), written c. 359: bishops cite the deposers of Paul as having said the Son is not coessential, and Athanasius, who had not seen the letter, explains it. No vendored source shows the point raised at Nicaea in 325.

prose_changes.old: The word homoousios - one substance - seems to have been rejected here as something Paul had misused, which is a large part of why its adoption at Nicaea in 325 was so contentious, and why Eastern bishops who were not Arians could still be uneasy about it.
prose_changes.new: The word homoousios - one substance - seems to have been rejected here as something Paul had misused. A generation after Nicaea adopted it in 325, Eastern bishops who were not Arians still cited this council when they balked at it.
prose_changes.reason: Same evidence as the why-field change: Athanasius, On the Councils 43 (npnf204 58972-58980) shows the council cited in the 350s by non-Arian bishops; nothing vendored shows it shaping the debate at Nicaea itself.

prose_changes.old: The Antiochene exegetical tradition that Diodore, Theodore and Chrysostom carry is usually traced back to Lucian's work on the text as well - which makes this century the origin of two things the next four centuries spent arguing about.
prose_changes.new: The Antiochene way of reading Scripture, carried by Diodore, Theodore and Chrysostom, may also go back to Lucian's work on the text. No ancient source draws that line. If it does, this century began two things the next four centuries spent arguing about.
prose_changes.reason: The existing link (Inferential-Thin) found no source tying Lucian to Diodore, Theodore or Chrysostom, and no repo-cited secondary work states the 'usually traced' consensus. The prose now matches the link.

prose_changes.old: Sits between latin-pastoral-congregational-christianity, which is Latin but Carthaginian, and homoian-arian-christianity, which is Danubian but a century later and beyond the floor. Its text reaches hieronymian-ascetic-literary by a route no other work in the corpus takes: Jerome edited it.
prose_changes.new: It sits between two neighbors. Latin pastoral Christianity at Carthage shares its language but not its region. Homoian Christianity shares its region: its leaders held sees in these provinces fifty years later. Its commentary on the Apocalypse reaches us as Jerome edited it.
prose_changes.reason: Raw movement ids and internal phrases ('beyond the floor', 'in the corpus') removed. 'A century later' contradicted the entry's own 'within fifty years' (Valens of Mursa and Ursacius of Singidunum, Athanasius Apol. c. Ar. 48). 'No other work takes this route' was a claim about the vendored collection, not about history; it is dropped.

prose_changes.old: Victorinus' recapitulation reading of the Apocalypse - that the seals, trumpets and bowls narrate the same events over again rather than a sequence of them - passed through Jerome's revision into Tyconius and Augustine and became the standard Western reading of the book.
prose_changes.new: Victorinus' recapitulation reading of the Apocalypse - that the seals, trumpets and bowls narrate the same events over again rather than a sequence of them - survived Jerome's revision. Tyconius and Augustine also taught readers to watch for recapitulation, though neither names Victorinus. It became the standard Western reading of the book.
prose_changes.reason: Tyconius wrote before Jerome's revision (he was condemned c. 380, per the vendored Burkitt edition's header), so the reading cannot have reached him through it. Tyconius's rule of recapitulation (tyconius_liber-regularum_burkitt1894.txt) and Augustine's account of it (De doctrina III.36, npnf102 53403) do not name Victorinus.

prose_changes.old: In 144 the Roman church expelled him and returned his money.
prose_changes.new: The Roman church expelled him and returned his money. The break is usually dated to 144. One recent study argues that date marks his arrival instead.
prose_changes.reason: Tertullian (Against Marcion IV.4, anf03 29239-29241; Prescription 30, anf03 21338-21340) documents the expulsion and the returned money but gives no year. The 144 date is Harnack's reckoning from Against Marcion I.19; Sebastian Moll, The Arch-Heretic Marcion (2010), cited in Build/worlds/pahc/CiC_W1_Doc01_World_Identification_FINAL.md, reads it as his arrival.

prose_changes.new: The Roman church expelled him, traditionally in 144, and returned his money. He then built
prose_changes.reason: Same evidence as the longDescription change: the year is a modern reckoning and is disputed (Moll 2010, cited in the pahc Doc_01).
